content: Inhaled anticholinergic medications, when used as the sole bronchodilator therapy, are one of the available treatment options for managing acute asthma in children. However, their effectiveness as a standalone treatment compared to other therapies has been evaluated. The objective of this analysis was to assess the efficacy of inhaled anticholinergic drugs administered alone, in comparison to a control, in children aged over two years experiencing acute asthma exacerbations. The review included only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) where anticholinergics were used as monotherapy and compared to placebo or other drugs or drug combinations. The search for relevant studies was conducted using the Cochrane Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) and the Cochrane Airways Group Register of trials, with the most recent search completed in April 2011. Two independent reviewers selected the trials, extracted data, and assessed the quality of the studies. Six studies met the inclusion criteria, but these studies were limited by small sample sizes, variations in treatment protocols, and differences in outcome measures. The overall quality of the studies was unclear. Data could only be pooled for specific outcomes, such as treatment failure and hospitalisation rates, while other outcomes could not be combined due to inconsistencies in measurement methods. Meta-analysis of the data revealed that children treated with anticholinergics alone were significantly more likely to experience treatment failure compared to those treated with beta2-agonists. This finding was based on four trials involving 171 children, with an odds ratio (OR) of 2.27 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.08 to 4.75). Similarly, treatment failure was more likely when anticholinergics were used alone compared to when they were combined with beta2-agonists, as shown in four trials involving 173 children (OR 2.65; 95% CI 1.2 to 5.88). Clinical scores and symptom measurements, which were assessed using different scales, showed conflicting results. However, individual trials reported that lung function outcomes were better in children who received a combination of anticholinergics and beta2-agonists compared to those who received anticholinergics alone. Importantly, the use of anticholinergic medications was not associated with significant adverse effects. In conclusion, for children over the age of two years with acute asthma exacerbations, inhaled anticholinergics used as single-agent bronchodilators were found to be less effective than beta2-agonists. Furthermore, they were also less effective than the combination of inhaled anticholinergics and beta2-agonists. Therefore, inhaled anticholinergic drugs alone are not recommended as a standalone treatment for children with acute asthma exacerbations.
